title: How Shark Attacks Work
summary: Shark Week edition of Stuff You Should Know on how shark attacks work. The hosts argue most attacks are mistaken identity (surfers resembling sea turtles or sea lions), and cover test bites, aggression, hunger, and feeding frenzies triggered by bleeding fish. They explain how sharks sense blood and electrical signals via the ampullae of Lorenzini, describe the three deadliest species (great white, tiger, bull), and recount attack stories including Kenny Dool's Oregon surfing attack, the USS Indianapolis sinking, and Rodney Fox's injuries. They discuss attack statistics (roughly 30 to 50 unprovoked attacks a year worldwide, 5 to 10 deaths, Florida leading), the availability heuristic, the coconut-death myth, safety precautions for swimmers and fishermen, the Jaws effect and its aftermath, and a French listener mail segment.

segments.title: Opening banter and Shark Week
segments.summary: Hosts open the Shark Week edition, joke about a Jaws DVD box set gift, and announce they will cover shark attacks. Sharks' bad reputation is said to be easing.

segments.title: Mistaken identity and test bites
segments.summary: Hosts argue most shark attacks are mistaken identity, since surfers can look like sea turtles or sea lions from below. They describe the great white test bite, then discuss aggression, confusion, and hunger as other causes.

segments.title: Blood, electrical sensing and feeding frenzies
segments.summary: Sharks can smell blood from far away, and dying fish generate electrical impulses detected by the ampullae of Lorenzini in the snout. Standing among dying fish can draw a shark to bite. Advice to punch the snout is discussed. Nurse sharks are described as bitten by divers who pull their tails.

segments.title: Deadliest sharks and attack stories
segments.summary: The three deadliest sharks are named as great white, tiger, and bull; bull sharks hit first and return, and attack in shallow water. The hosts recount Don Shauman's bull shark attack and Kenny Dool's 1979 Oregon surfing attack, where his surfboard saved him.

segments.title: USS Indianapolis and shark injuries
segments.summary: The hosts describe tiger sharks circling the wounded, then the USS Indianapolis sinking in 1945, where sharks killed many of the roughly 1,000 survivors of the sinking before rescue. They describe injuries, limb loss, and Rodney Fox's 1963 near Adelaide, Australia attack.

segments.title: Why the big three are dangerous and shark statistics
segments.summary: Hosts say the big three sharks are top predators not afraid of humans, while other species also bite. They give attack statistics: 30 to 50 unprovoked attacks a year worldwide, most in the US and especially Florida, 5 to 10 deaths a year. They explain that more beachgoers explain rising numbers and discuss San Francisco sea lions.

segments.title: Availability heuristic and coconut myth
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how sensational media reports make shark attacks seem more common, the availability heuristic, and the myth that shark attacks are compared to deaths from falling coconuts, which the hosts call urban legend.

segments.title: Shark attack safety precautions
segments.summary: Advice includes avoiding dusk and dawn, murky water, open cuts, sandbars and drop-offs, bright or contrasting swimwear, shiny jewelry, thrashing, areas with seals, and fishing with bait near the body. If attacked, fight back by punching the snout or hitting the eyes.

segments.title: Jaws effect and shark conservation
segments.summary: Hosts describe the Jaws effect: fear of the ocean and shark fishing tournaments, then Peter Benchley's regret and conservation. The marine biologist's view that the film spurred shark research funding and inspired biologists, with Matt Hooper as a role model.

segments.title: French listener mail
segments.summary: A listener named Sylvain writes in from France, now in Minneapolis, about his brother Pierre Yves and the podcast. Hosts read it and mention other French listeners.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact info
segments.summary: Hosts invite feedback on Twitter, Facebook, and email, encourage viewing Shark Week, and close the episode.
